subject: principles-of-flight
source_policy: Use the approved POF handbook as technical source of truth. Question-bank and mock-exam material may confirm exam wording/mapping but must not override handbook physics.

concepts.concept: At the same angle of attack and airspeed, lowering trailing-edge flaps increases wing camber and lift, while also increasing drag.
concepts.reuse_justification: All four questions test the same flap effect: more lift at a given angle of attack and airspeed, with increased drag.

source.notes: The handbook describes flap extension as changing the wing lifting characteristics and increasing lift and drag.

brief.student_must_understand: For the same baseline angle of attack and airspeed, flap extension increases camber, producing more lift and more drag.
preserve: Same relative-wind reference in both panels
refine: Compare FLAP UP versus FLAP DOWN side by side
Make lift and drag vector increases immediately readable
Do not imply all flap types increase wing area

concepts.mapping_reason: The four target questions directly ask what trailing-edge flaps do to lift and drag at a given flight condition.

concepts.concept: For the same weight and load factor, flap extension increases maximum lift capability and therefore lowers the indicated speed at which the wing stalls.
concepts.reuse_justification: Both questions test the same operational result of flap extension: stall speed decreases.

source.location: Chapter 2, Flight Control Systems / Wing Flaps
source.notes: The handbook states that flaps change wing lifting characteristics and decrease the speed at which the wing stalls.

brief.student_must_understand: With weight and load factor held constant, the higher lift capability available with flaps lowers stall speed.
refine: Use paired lift-capability curves or a clear before/after comparison
Keep critical-angle messaging separate from the speed result
Avoid implying bank angle has no stall-speed effect

concepts.mapping_reason: Both target questions ask whether flap extension raises or lowers stall speed; the visual teaches that exact relationship.

concepts.concept: A Fowler flap extends rearward as well as downward, increasing effective wing area in addition to increasing camber.

source.notes: The handbook distinguishes the Fowler flap by its rearward travel, which increases wing area as it extends.

brief.student_must_understand: Unlike a simple hinged flap, a Fowler flap slides aft before/down as it extends, increasing effective wing area.
refine: Make the aft translation visually dominant
Show the planform/chord-area increase with a simple dimension cue
Do not generalize the area increase to all flap types

concepts.mapping_reason: Question 1358 specifically tests the Fowler flap's area-increasing rearward extension.

concepts.concept: Static stability describes the initial tendency after a disturbance; dynamic stability describes what the subsequent oscillations do over time.
concepts.reuse_justification: The three questions are one response-system concept: initial restoring tendency versus damping or growth of oscillations over time.

source.location: Chapter 1, Static and Dynamic Stability / Figures 1-19 and 1-20
source.notes: The handbook separates initial static response from the time history of dynamic oscillation and damping.

brief.student_must_understand: An aeroplane can initially tend back toward trim yet still be dynamically unstable if each oscillation grows; a dynamically stable response damps toward trim.
refine: Keep static and dynamic labels semantically separate

concepts.mapping_reason: The questions distinguish stable return, dynamically stable passenger-aircraft behavior, and statically stable but dynamically unstable growing oscillations.

concepts.concept: A vertical fin or keel area behind the centre of gravity acts like a weather vane: sideslip creates a tail sideforce that produces a restoring yawing moment.
concepts.reuse_justification: Both questions test the same directional-stability mechanism: aft vertical side area produces a restoring yaw moment, and more aft keel/fin area strengthens it.

source.notes: The handbook describes the vertical fin behind the CG as a weather-vane surface that returns a yawed aeroplane toward its original direction.

brief.student_must_understand: When the aeroplane yaws away from the relative wind, airflow on the fin behind the CG produces a restoring moment; increasing aft vertical area increases directional stability.
refine: Show sideforce on the fin with the correct restoring yaw direction
Use a small-area versus larger-area comparison inset
Do not show rudder deflection because this is stability, not pilot control
add: More aft side area = stronger stability

concepts.mapping_reason: The target questions directly ask what provides directional stability and why increasing keel surface behind the CG increases it.
